name: Learn: Pod Design (hardened)
objective: CKAD › Application Design and Build + Observability. Drill EVERY pod-design corner harder than the exam: classic vs native sidecars, init ordering, all three probe types and handlers, lifecycle hooks + graceful shutdown, full securityContext hardening, QoS classes, the Downward API, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.
description: Nine strict practicals covering the whole pod-design surface. Each Check shows which requirements you met and the exact reason for any you missed.

questions.title: Classic sidecar sharing an emptyDir
questions.teach:
A **sidecar** is a second container in the same pod that augments the main one (logging, proxy, sync). Containers in a pod share the network and any **shared volume** — an `emptyDir` is the usual scratch space (lives and dies with the pod).

- `emptyDir: {}` — node disk; `emptyDir: {medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 64Mi}` — tmpfs RAM-backed.
- Each container mounts the **same volume name** at its own `mountPath` (paths can differ).
- Containers start in parallel (unlike initContainers) and share the volume immediately.

**Gotchas:** the volume only matters if **both** containers mount it; a typo in the volume name = two separate volumes; an emptyDir is **not** shared across pods or restarts of the pod (only container restarts).
questions.prompt:
Create pod `sidecar-pod` in namespace `pod-design` with two containers sharing an `emptyDir`:
- `writer` (image `busybox:1.36`) running `sh -c 'while true; do date >> /data/out.log; sleep 1; done'`
- `reader` (image `busybox:1.36`) running `sh -c 'tail -F /data/out.log'`

Both mount the shared emptyDir at `/data`.
questions.hint: Define one `volumes: [{name: data, emptyDir: {}}]` and give BOTH containers `volumeMounts: [{name: data, mountPath: /data}]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: sidecar-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: writer
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","while true; do date >> /data/out.log; sleep 1; done"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: data, mountPath: /data } ]
  - name: reader
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /data/out.log"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: data, mountPath: /data } ]
  volumes: [ { name: data, emptyDir: {} } ]
YAML

verification.description: sidecar-pod: writer + reader share one emptyDir at /data

questions.title: Init containers run to completion, in order
questions.teach:
**initContainers** run **sequentially, to completion**, before any app container starts — each must exit 0 before the next begins. Used to prepare data, wait for a dependency, or run migrations.

- Listed under `spec.initContainers`; they share volumes with the app containers.
- If an init container fails, the pod restarts it (per `restartPolicy`) and the app never starts — a stuck pod in `Init:0/2` means the first init container is failing.
- App containers only start once **all** init containers have succeeded.

**Gotchas:** order matters (top to bottom); a long/hanging init container blocks the whole pod; init containers can have their own resources/securityContext.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `init-pod` in `pod-design`:
- init container `init-a` (`busybox:1.36`) runs `sh -c 'echo a > /work/a'`
- then init container `init-b` (`busybox:1.36`) runs `sh -c 'echo b > /work/b'`
- main container `app` (`busybox:1.36`) runs `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`

All three mount the same `emptyDir` at `/work`, and the init containers must be ordered `init-a` then `init-b`.
questions.hint: `spec.initContainers` is an ordered list — put `init-a` before `init-b`. Share one emptyDir named e.g. `work` mounted at `/work` in all three containers.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: init-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: init-a
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","echo a > /work/a"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ]
  - name: init-b
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","echo b > /work/b"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ]
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ]
  volumes: [ { name: work, emptyDir: {} } ]
YAML

verification.description: init-pod: init-a then init-b (ordered) + app, sharing emptyDir at /work

questions.title: Native sidecar (initContainer with restartPolicy: Always)
questions.teach:
Since Kubernetes 1.29 a **native sidecar** is an **initContainer with `restartPolicy: Always`**. Unlike a classic sidecar (a normal container), a native sidecar:
- **starts before** the main app containers and **stays running** alongside them,
- is guaranteed to be up before the app starts (great for proxies/log shippers),
- is **not** counted toward pod completion (a Job pod can finish while the sidecar runs).

It lives in `spec.initContainers` but with `restartPolicy: Always` on that container — that one field is what makes it a long-lived sidecar instead of a run-once init container.

**Gotchas:** only the native-sidecar initContainer gets `restartPolicy: Always`; a normal init container has none. This is the modern fix for the old 'sidecar keeps a Job from completing' problem.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `log-pod` in `pod-design` with a **native sidecar**:
- initContainer `logger` (`busybox:1.36`) with `restartPolicy: Always`, running `sh -c 'tail -F /var/log/app.log'`
- main container `app` (`busybox:1.36`) running `sh -c 'while true; do echo hi >> /var/log/app.log; sleep 2; done'`

Share an `emptyDir` at `/var/log` in both.
questions.hint: Put `logger` under `spec.initContainers` with `restartPolicy: Always` set ON that container. Share an emptyDir named e.g. `logs` at `/var/log`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: log-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: logger
    image: busybox:1.36
    restartPolicy: Always
    command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /var/log/app.log"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log } ]
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","while true; do echo hi >> /var/log/app.log; sleep 2; done"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log } ]
  volumes: [ { name: logs, emptyDir: {} } ]
YAML

verification.description: log-pod: native sidecar 'logger' (initContainer restartPolicy:Always) + app sharing /var/log

questions.title: All three probe types, three handlers
questions.teach:
Three probe kinds, each with a different job:
- **livenessProbe** — restarts the container if it fails (deadlock recovery).
- **readinessProbe** — removes the pod from Service endpoints while it fails (no traffic), but doesn't restart it.
- **startupProbe** — gates liveness/readiness until a slow app has started; while it runs, the others are suspended.

Three **handlers** work in any probe: `httpGet` (path+port), `exec` (command, exit 0 = healthy), `tcpSocket` (port opens). Plus timing: `initialDelaySeconds`, `periodSeconds`, `timeoutSeconds`, `failureThreshold`, `successThreshold` (readiness can be >1; liveness must be 1).

**Gotchas:** a too-aggressive livenessProbe (short period/low threshold) causes restart loops; use a **startupProbe** for slow starters instead of a huge `initialDelaySeconds`; readiness failing ≠ restart.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `health-pod` in `pod-design` (`nginx:1.25`, one container `web`) with all three probes:
- **livenessProbe**: `exec` running `["sh","-c","ls /usr/share/nginx/html"]`, `periodSeconds=15`.
- **readinessProbe**: `httpGet` path `/` port `80`, `initialDelaySeconds=5`.
- **startupProbe**: `tcpSocket` port `80`, `failureThreshold=30`, `periodSeconds=10`.
questions.hint: All three go under the same container. Use `exec.command` for liveness, `httpGet` for readiness, `tcpSocket` for startup — mind the exact timing fields.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: health-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    livenessProbe:
      exec: { command: ["sh","-c","ls /usr/share/nginx/html"] }
      periodSeconds: 15
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
    startupProbe:
      tcpSocket: { port: 80 }
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
YAML

questions.title: Lifecycle hooks + graceful shutdown
questions.teach:
**Lifecycle hooks** run code at container start/stop:
- `postStart` — fires right after the container starts (no ordering guarantee vs the entrypoint; both run concurrently).
- `preStop` — fires **before** SIGTERM on shutdown; the container has until `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to finish (preStop + SIGTERM handling must fit inside it) before SIGKILL.

Graceful shutdown sequence: pod marked Terminating → removed from endpoints → `preStop` runs → SIGTERM → (grace period) → SIGKILL.

**Gotchas:** a `preStop` that sleeps longer than `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` gets cut off by SIGKILL; `postStart` failing kills the container; hooks support `exec` and `httpGet` handlers.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `graceful-pod` in `pod-design` (`nginx:1.25`, container `web`) with:
- `lifecycle.postStart` exec `["sh","-c","echo started > /tmp/poststart"]`
- `lifecycle.preStop` exec `["sh","-c","nginx -s quit"]`
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`
questions.hint: `lifecycle.postStart.exec.command` and `lifecycle.preStop.exec.command` live on the container; `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` lives on the pod `spec`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: graceful-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    lifecycle:
      postStart: { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","echo started > /tmp/poststart"] } }
      preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","nginx -s quit"] } }
YAML

verification.description: graceful-pod: postStart + preStop exec hooks + terminationGracePeriodSeconds 30

questions.title: Full securityContext hardening (pod + container)
questions.teach:
`securityContext` exists at **pod level** and **container level** (container overrides pod for overlapping fields). Know which field lives where:
- **Pod-only:** `fsGroup` (group owner of mounted volumes), `supplementalGroups`.
- **Container-only:** `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `capabilities` (add/drop), `allowPrivilegeEscalation`, `privileged`.
- **Either (container wins):** `runAsUser`, `runAsGroup`, `runAsNonRoot`, `seccompProfile`.

**Canonical hardening:** `runAsNonRoot: true` + a non-zero `runAsUser`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` with an `emptyDir` for every path the app writes, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and `capabilities: {drop: [ALL]}` then add back only what's needed.

**Gotchas:** `readOnlyRootFilesystem` + no writable mount = the app can't write and may crash; `runAsNonRoot: true` with an image that defaults to root (or `runAsUser: 0`) fails to start; capabilities and readOnlyRootFilesystem **cannot** be set at pod level.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `secure-pod` in `pod-design` (`busybox:1.36`, container `app`, running `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`) with:
- **Pod-level**: `fsGroup: 2000`, `runAsNonRoot: true`.
- **Container-level**: `runAsUser: 1000`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, capabilities `drop: [ALL]` and `add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]`.
- An `emptyDir` mounted at `/tmp` (so the read-only-root container has a writable path).
questions.hint: `fsGroup` + `runAsNonRoot` go under `spec.securityContext` (pod). `runAsUser`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation`, `capabilities` go under the container's `securityContext`. Add an emptyDir volume mounted at /tmp.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: secure-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  securityContext:
    fsGroup: 2000
    runAsNonRoot: true
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    securityContext:
      runAsUser: 1000
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"], add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"] }
    volumeMounts: [ { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp } ]
  volumes: [ { name: tmp, emptyDir: {} } ]
YAML

verification.description: container: readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation false, drop ALL + add NET_BIND_SERVICE, emptyDir at /tmp

questions.title: Quality of Service: make a Guaranteed pod
questions.teach:
Kubernetes assigns each pod a **QoS class** from its resources — it decides eviction order under node pressure: - **Guaranteed** — every container sets `requests == limits` for **both** cpu and memory. Evicted last. - **Burstable** — at least one request/limit set, but not equal/complete. Evicted after BestEffort. - **BestEffort** — no requests or limits at all. Evicted first (and OOMKilled first). `requests` drive scheduling; `limits` cap usage (memory over limit → **OOMKilled**; cpu over limit → throttled). QoS is computed, not set directly — you get Guaranteed by making requests exactly equal limits. **Gotchas:** if you set only limits, Kubernetes copies them to requests (still Guaranteed if both cpu+mem); a single container missing a limit drops the whole pod to Burstable; check with `kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'`.
questions.prompt: Create pod `qos-pod` in `pod-design` (`busybox:1.36`, container `app`, `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`) whose QoS class is **Guaranteed** — set requests and limits **equal**: cpu `200m`, memory `256Mi` for both.
questions.hint: Set `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` to the SAME values (cpu=200m, memory=256Mi). Verify: `kubectl -n pod-design get pod qos-pod -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'` → Guaranteed.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: qos-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
      limits: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
YAML

questions.title: Downward API: expose pod metadata
questions.teach:
The **Downward API** exposes pod/container metadata to the app without hardcoding it — as env vars or files.
- **Env via `fieldRef`:** pod fields like `metadata.name`, `metadata.namespace`, `status.podIP`, `spec.nodeName`.
- **Env via `resourceFieldRef`:** a container's `requests`/`limits`, e.g. `limits.cpu`, `requests.memory` (with an optional `divisor`).
- **Volume (`downwardAPI`):** project fields/labels/annotations into files (the only way to expose **labels/annotations**, which `fieldRef` env can't do).

**Gotchas:** `metadata.labels`/`annotations` are only available via a **volume**, not env `fieldRef`; `resourceFieldRef` needs the resource to actually be set on the container; mounted downward-API files update when labels/annotations change (env does not).
questions.prompt:
Create pod `downward-pod` in `pod-design` (`busybox:1.36`, container `app`, `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`), labelled `app=downward`, with cpu limit `500m`, exposing:
- env `POD_NAME` ← `metadata.name`, env `POD_NS` ← `metadata.namespace`
- env `CPU_LIMIT` ← `resourceFieldRef` `limits.cpu`
- a `downwardAPI` **volume** mounted at `/podinfo` with an item `labels` ← `metadata.labels`
questions.hint: Env uses `valueFrom.fieldRef` (for metadata.*) and `valueFrom.resourceFieldRef` (for limits.cpu, needs `containerName`). The labels file needs a `downwardAPI` volume with `items: [{path: labels, fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.labels}}]`, mounted at /podinfo.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: downward-pod, namespace: pod-design, labels: { app: downward } }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources: { limits: { cpu: 500m } }
    env:
    - name: POD_NAME
      valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } }
    - name: POD_NS
      valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.namespace } }
    - name: CPU_LIMIT
      valueFrom: { resourceFieldRef: { containerName: app, resource: limits.cpu } }
    volumeMounts: [ { name: podinfo, mountPath: /podinfo } ]
  volumes:
  - name: podinfo
    downwardAPI:
      items: [ { path: labels, fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.labels } } ]
YAML

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a Deployment that won't go Ready
questions.teach:
On the exam and in real life you'll get something **already broken** with no description of the fault — you diagnose it. Method: - `kubectl get deploy/pods` — see the symptom (0 available, `Running` but `0/1 READY`, `CrashLoopBackOff`…). - `kubectl describe pod

` — read **Events** and the probe/section details (readiness probe failures show here). - `kubectl logs

` (`-p` for a crashed previous instance). Common readiness faults: probe on the **wrong port/path**, wrong scheme, too-short `initialDelaySeconds`. A pod that's `Running` but never `Ready` is almost always a **readiness probe** pointing at something that doesn't answer. **Gotchas:** fix the controller (Deployment), not the pod (pods are immutable for probes); after fixing, the Deployment rolls new pods — confirm with `kubectl rollout status`.
questions.prompt:
Deployment `diag` in `pod-design` has 1 replica but it **never becomes Ready** (`kubectl -n pod-design get deploy diag` shows `0/1`). Diagnose the fault and fix it so the Deployment reports an available replica. Don't delete and rebuild from scratch — find and fix what's wrong.

Target: Deployment `diag` has at least 1 available replica.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n pod-design describe pod -l app=diag` → the readiness probe is failing. Compare the probe's port to the port the container (`nginx:1.25`) actually serves on. Fix the Deployment's readiness probe (`kubectl -n pod-design edit deploy diag`), then watch `rollout status`.
questions.solution:
# The readiness probe targets port 8080, but nginx serves on 80.
kubectl -n pod-design patch deployment diag --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe/httpGet/port","value":80}]'
kubectl -n pod-design rollout status deployment/diag

verification.description: Deployment diag has >=1 available replica (readiness fault fixed)
